question_text: X took up distance running seriously in his thirties, in the late 1940s, and within about two years was the best runner at his local athletic club. Asked by the club secretary why he punished himself so hard in training, he said his job was so stressful that running flat out was the only way to get it out of his head. In 1947 he ran a marathon in 2 hours, 46 minutes and 3 seconds. That race doubled as a trial for the British team for the following summer's Olympics in London. He was injured on the day, finished fifth, and that was the end of any chance of selection. His personal best was about eleven minutes slower than the time that won the Olympic marathon in 1948, and would have put him around fifteenth in that field. At Cambridge his usual route had been to Ely and back, some fifty kilometres. Later, rather than take the train to meetings in London, he would sometimes run the forty miles instead. Identify X.

In Bawa Mohtara, a village in Bemetara district of Chhattisgarh, he had been a fixture for longer than anyone living could remember. Generations grew up with him. The village looked after him, fed him, and thought of him as a kind of guardian, proof, they felt, that the place was blessed. They called him, with great affection, Gangaram. His story is now taught in schools, it has been made a chapter in an NCERT textbook. He died on 8 January 2019, at an age the village put at about 130. Nobody in Bawa Mohtara ate that day. More than five hundred people came, from there and from all the villages around, and walked behind the truck that carried him to his grave, which they had covered in flowers and garlands. Grown men wept, and the tears were real. There is talk, still, of building him a temple. Who is Gangaram?

You can probably call Jay Jackson the Iftekhar or Jagdish Raj of Hollywood, except that instead of playing a policeman in every film, it is a journalist. He has around 50 screen credits with more than 70 per cent of them playing a reporter or a news anchor with no name, 'Reporter', 'News Anchor', 'Male Newscaster #1'. It helps that he actually was one: 22 years as a TV news anchor and reporter in Southern California before he acted in anything. The exception is the one role he is known for: a TV journalist who actually has a name, played across six seasons of one show, and played again when that cast reassembled for a one-off reunion, five years after it ended. Name the character. Dexter (2007) - Reporter - 1 episode. The Mentalist (2010) - Reporter - 1 episode. Fast Five (2011) - Field Reporter - film. Battleship (2012) - American Newscaster - film. Without Remorse (2021) - Political Analyst - film. 9-1-1: Lone Star (2021) - Newscaster - 1 episode. Inventing Anna (2022) - News Anchor - 1 episode. The Brothers Sun (2024) - TV Reporter - 1 episode. Loot (2024) - Journalist - 1 episode. Interior Chinatown (2024) - News Anchor #3 - 1 episode. Plus recurring news-anchor stints on Scandal and Supergirl.

Known by his patronymic sobriquet, X (literally, 'son of a duckling'), was made ambassador to the Mongol court in China in 1342 by Muhammad bin Tughluq. He had spent the preceding years as the Sultan's qazi of Delhi, and had been poor at it: he spoke the local language badly and followed the Maliki school of law in a Hanafi city, so two deputies did the work and brought him the papers to sign. The embassy set out with an escort of about a thousand men and gifts that included two hundred slaves and a hundred horses. Rebels ambushed the party outside Delhi; X was robbed, separated from his companions and nearly killed. At Calicut, while he was ashore at a mosque, a storm sank one of his ships with the slaves and the horses aboard, and the other sailed away without him and was seized months later by a Sumatran king. Rather than return and explain himself to the Sultan, X ran to the Maldives, where he was promptly made chief judge again. Identify X.

Connect. Three picture clues were shown: a Henri Matisse paper cutout artwork titled 'Icarus' (a black falling silhouette with a red heart, set against a blue background with yellow starbursts); a photograph of a bearded stand-up comedian performing on stage, shown at two different venues (one photo in a grey Pearl Jam t-shirt, the other in a teal shirt in front of a comedy club backdrop); and the poster artwork for a documentary film, showing a giant red hand controlling a running silhouetted figure by puppet strings.

Lose/Lose, released by Zach Gage in 2009 for the Mac, looks like Space Invaders. Your ship sits at the bottom, rows of aliens drift down the screen, and you score points for every alien you shoot. The aliens never shoot back. They only drift, and if one reaches you, your run is over. It is difficult to download the game, in the first instance, considering it is flagged by most antivirus programs. On top of that, you can only play the game once. Once a player loses, the game deletes itself. Not a game-over screen and a reset, the application removes itself from your hard drive. The game is flagged as a Trojan by most antivirus programs. Apart from the fact you can only play it once, why is the game called Lose/Lose? What happens when you try to win it?
answer_text: Each alien on screen corresponds to a real file on your computer, and shooting one permanently deletes that file. So you lose either way: lose the game and the application deletes itself, or 'win' by shooting aliens and you permanently delete your own files.

question_text: These paintings are by X, who walked away from music at the end of the 1980s and has been exhibiting and selling paintings as an artist since 2000. The images shown include a whimsical painting of a white rabbit holding carrots, and a painting titled 'Trust' of a young girl in a blue dress reaching out to a white rabbit. Identify X.

In October 2002, in a seventh-season episode of Buffy the Vampire Slayer called 'Help', Willow asks Buffy about a girl the two of them are worried about, and in her one-line question, brings something into normal parlance for the first time in pop culture. Over the next four years, there were many attempts to try and stop people from this usage. In February 2003, a cease-and-desist was sent to a man who ran a site cataloguing new coinages. In October 2006, a public appeal was made asking everyone to stop. But it was too late already. By that June, the Oxford English Dictionary had admitted it, and Merriam-Webster followed a month later. What are we talking about?

This chart ran in Quartz India in November 2014, drawn from a year of figures covering September 2013 to September 2014. Each bar is an Indian holiday, measured as a percentage change against the ordinary Indian baseline. Diwali is the steepest fall on the chart, down nearly 36%, with Dussehra, New Year's Eve and Gandhi Jayanti behind it. Four days run the other way: Rakhi, Republic Day, Independence Day and Eid-ul-Fitr, the last of them up 9%. The piece around the chart adds that in an ordinary week Saturday is the high and Sunday the low, the reverse of the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Brazil, where Monday is the busiest day. What data is this chart depicting?

20 Fenchurch Street, pictured, is a 38-storey office tower in the City of London, designed by Rafael Vinoly and completed in 2014. It widens as it rises, and its south face curves inward. In the summer of 2013, before it was finished, that curve worked as a concave mirror. For about two hours a day it focused the sun onto the street below, hot enough to melt panels on a parked Jaguar and let a reporter fry an egg on the pavement. It was fixed permanently the following year with a shading awning along the south face, and the building has been harmless ever since. The press had a fortnight of fun with it. One of the names they coined was the Fryscraper. The other stuck much harder, and is still what the whole episode is called, a pun on the nickname Londoners had already given the building, which comes from its silhouette. What was that second name?
answer_text: The Walkie-Scorchie (a pun on the building's nickname, the Walkie-Talkie)

question_text: X was invented on a farm around a century ago, for the most ordinary of reasons: to stop good food going to waste. The scraps left at the end of the day's work were too small and too ragged to sell on their own, so they were gathered up, packed into a pouch made from the same material, loosened with cream, and the top pinched shut. The result was then bundled in asphodel leaves and tied into a topknot. The leaves kept it moist and doubled as a label, while they were still green, the contents were still good. X spoils fast even today, and is sold as something to eat within a few days of being made. X literally translates to 'buttery' or 'buttered'. Identify X.

In 1851, during a break at the first international chess tournament in London, Adolf Anderssen and Lionel Kieseritzky sat down to a casual game that counted for nothing. Anderssen gave away a bishop, then both rooks, then his queen, and delivered mate with three minor pieces. Kieseritzky was taken enough with it to telegraph the moves to his club in Paris and then publish them. In 1855 another player christened it the Immortal Game, and it has been called that ever since. In a film from the early eighties, its finish is replayed. Two characters are playing remotely, each at his own board, one of them in a tower high above the city, the other in an apartment far below. A third man stands at the second player's shoulder and feeds him the moves, the queen sacrifice among them, and the game is the pretext that gets that third man into the tower. Identify the film.

By the autumn of 1963, X was dying of cancer at his home in Los Angeles, and near the end he could no longer speak. He had spent his last decade arguing for psychedelics. A book of his from 1954 had described a mescaline trip in close detail, and he had taken LSD steadily through the years that followed. On the morning of 22 November he wrote his wife Laura a note: 'LSD, 100 micrograms, intramuscular.' She injected him at 11:20, and again an hour later. At twenty past five that evening his breathing stopped. Laura wrote afterwards that everyone in the room agreed it was the most serene, the most beautiful death they had seen, and that the doctors and the nurse said they had never watched anyone in that physical condition go without pain and without struggle. The death of a writer of his standing should have run on front pages everywhere. It barely registered. Identify X (5 points), and say why his death went almost unreported (5 points).
answer_text: Aldous Huxley. He died on the same day as JFK's assassination (22 November 1963), so his death was overshadowed in the news.

question_text: In the mid 18th century, a British army surgeon posted to North America set some mocking verses to an old Irish tune. The sentiment is plain contempt: these colonials are rustics, and the smallest affectation is enough to convince them they are men of fashion. One of the words used in the song, two centuries of children have heard that word and assumed the line is about pasta, it isn't, refers to a certain kind of young Englishman, one home from a tour of the Continent in Italian tailoring and a tower of powdered hair, insufferable about his own good taste. A fop. The Americans took the song for themselves, added verses, and sang it back at the British. It is now a state song. What song?
answer_text: Yankee Doodle. 'Stuck a feather in his cap and called it macaroni' - a macaroni was a fop, not a pasta.

question_text: In Dungeons & Dragons, Xs (see picture, an image of a large, hairy, tusked humanoid monster wielding a spiked club) are a class of monsters that are distantly related to, but larger and stronger than, goblins and hobgoblins. Classified as goblinoids, they are hairy and tall (around 7 feet), and have a reputation for being dim-witted and brutish. The name X comes from English folklore, where it is recorded from the 1570s. Invented by adults to frighten children into being obedient, they were said to live in the woods and to carry off children who misbehaved. In today's parlance, X has lost the horror and kept the nuisance. It is now used to describe a persistent source of irritation or annoyance, a pet peeve. Identify X.

A 17-second video clip was shown of a point from a tennis match on a clay court. This clip was not recorded by any camera operator. No camera in the venue moved, and nobody framed the shot. Hundreds of small, cheap video sensors are fixed around the court, and software reconstructs the scene in three dimensions in real time, generating any angle on demand. The Oslo company that built it calls the result a weightless camera, and has run it at the Miami, Madrid and US Opens. The company is named X, after a 19th-century photographer. One of its founders has said he sees a resemblance between what they do and what that man did with sequenced triggers to create motion: in the 1870s he set a line of cameras along one side of a track and had the subject passing them trip each shutter in turn, to settle a dispute about movement that the eye could not resolve. What came back is often called the first moving picture. Name this Norwegian company.
answer_text: Muybridge (named after the photographer Eadweard Muybridge)

question_text: In 1977, a Japanese company merged with a fishing-tackle maker and a manufacturer of athletic uniforms. It had been founded in Kobe nearly thirty years before that, and had spent those years outfitting athletes from the ground up. The combined business took a new name, and that name is an acronym, almost, of a Latin motto. Almost, because the Latin motto in question translates as 'a sound mind in a sound body', while the company's version replaces it with a sound soul in a sound body. Name the company.
answer_text: Asics. From 'Anima Sana In Corpore Sano'; Juvenal's original phrase used 'mens' instead of 'anima', which would have given MSICS instead.
